prompt: You tested six settings and reported only the best one. How many trials count?

options.text: 1, the setting that was reported.
6, because every setting tested counts.
5, because the discarded settings do not count.
0, because nothing was reported in full.

explanations.a: Reporting one setting hides the other five trials. The search size is part of the honest result.
explanations.c: Discarded settings are trials too. They must be counted, even when they are not reported.
explanations.d: The trials happened, so they count. Hiding them does not remove them.

prompt: Hypothetical. A grid has 6 lookbacks, 5 ATR multiples and 3 filters. How many combinations does the grid contain?
Hypothetical. A grid has 90 tests, and each test has a 5% chance of looking good by luck. About how many lucky results should you expect?
solution: Expected lucky results = 90 x 0.05 = 4.5. So about 4 or 5 lucky results. Check: 5% of 90 is 90 / 20 = 4.5.

prompt: The best setting on the in-sample data is most likely to do what on new data?

options.text: Repeat its in-sample result exactly.
Do worse than it did on the data used to choose it, on average.
Do better on new data, because it was the best.
Show the same result, because the data is the same.

explanations.a: The in-sample best is biased upward. It was picked because it looked best on that data, so it is unlikely to repeat exactly.
explanations.c: Being the best on one data set does not make a setting the best on new data. The result often falls.
explanations.d: The new data is not the same as the data used to choose. It is the held-out data, and the result there is the honest test.

prompt: Hypothetical. You tried 30 variants and show one of them. A friend asks how many tests were run. What is the honest answer?

options.text: One, the variant that is shown.
30, and the report should say so.
Only the variants that passed the pass rule.
It depends on the chart.

explanations.a: Showing one variant does not reduce the number of tests. All 30 were run.
explanations.c: Counting only the passing variants hides the failed ones. The honest count includes every variant tried.
explanations.d: The number of tests does not depend on the chart. It is the count of variants tried.

prompt: Here is a report: Best cell: Rs 12,000 profit. Settings: 5 lookbacks by 4 multiples. Which part is wrong?

options.text: The report hides the other cells and does not state the number of combinations as the trial count.
The best cell is always the one to trust.
Grids are never useful in a test.
Reporting one result is always best practice.

explanations.b: The best cell was picked because it looked best. That is the reason to be careful with it.
explanations.c: Grids are useful for seeing how the results change with settings. The problem is the report, not the grid.
explanations.d: Reporting one result hides the search that produced it. The full grid and the count of trials should be shown.

prompt: You changed a setting just to see what would happen, and you did not write it down. Does it count?

options.text: No, untracked changes do not count.
Yes, it is a trial and belongs in the count.
No, only saved files count.
Only if the result was good.

explanations.a: A change tried in a test is a trial, whether or not it was recorded. Not recording it hides the search.
explanations.c: The test ran, so the trial happened. Saved files do not decide whether a trial counts.
explanations.d: A trial counts whatever its result. Counting only good results is the bias this chapter describes.
